recipe.name: Aloo Paratha
steps: Reserve 200 ml water for dough. Simmer whole potatoes in the remaining water for 20–25 minutes until a knife passes through; drain, peel and cool.
Knead 300 g flour, 4 g salt and the reserved 200 ml water into soft dough; cover 20 minutes. Keep 30 g flour for rolling.
Mash potatoes without lumps. Mix in finely chopped chilli and coriander, cumin, mango powder, chilli powder and remaining salt; let steam escape completely.
Divide dough and filling into eight equal portions. Roll each dough ball into a small disc, place filling centrally and pinch the edges closed.
Flatten seam-side down. Dust lightly with the reserved flour and roll gently to about 16 cm, keeping the filling evenly enclosed.
Heat a heavy tawa over medium-high heat. Cook a paratha for 60–90 seconds until bubbles appear, then turn and brush with a little ghee.
Turn again, grease the second side and press the edges. Cook 2–3 minutes more until browned on both sides with no damp dough at the edges.
tips: Keep unused dough covered so the surface does not dry out.
recipe.notes: Makes eight breads, two per serving. Serve freshly cooked with a curry or curd.

recipe.name: Bhatura
steps: Mix 300 g flour with sugar, salt, baking powder and baking soda. Reserve 30 g flour for rolling; measure 20 ml oil from the total.
Add curd and 20 ml oil. Add water gradually and knead 8 minutes into a smooth, soft dough; cover and rest for 2 hours.
Divide into eight smooth balls. Dust sparingly and roll each into an even oval about 3 mm thick; thick edges prevent full puffing.
Heat the remaining oil in a deep heavy pan to 180°C, leaving ample space above the oil. Fry one bread at a time.
Slide in a bhatura carefully and gently press with a slotted spoon until it puffs. Turn after 30–45 seconds and fry the other side golden.
Lift and drain on a rack. Adjust heat between batches to keep the oil near 180°C; serve immediately while puffed and soft inside.
tips: Keep unused dough covered so the surface does not dry out.
recipe.notes: Makes eight bhature. Oil is the frying medium; the full quantity is not consumed. This version uses chemical leavening.

recipe.name: Missi Roti
steps: Finely chop onion, chilli and coriander. Mix gram flour with 150 g wheat flour, carom seeds, turmeric and salt; reserve 30 g wheat flour for rolling.
Add chopped vegetables and 10 g ghee. Add water gradually, kneading a soft but non-sticky dough; cover for 20 minutes.
Divide into eight portions and smooth each ball. Dust lightly with reserved flour and roll to 14–15 cm; keep the edges evenly thick.
Place a roti on a medium-hot heavy tawa. Cook about 90 seconds until the surface loses its wet shine and small bubbles form.
Turn, spread a little remaining ghee and cook another minute. Turn again and press around the edges until both sides develop brown spots.
Check one torn edge: there should be no moist flour layer or raw gram-flour smell. Cook remaining rotis and keep covered loosely until serving.
tips: Keep unused dough covered so the surface does not dry out.
recipe.notes: Makes eight breads, two per serving. Serve freshly cooked with a curry or curd.

recipe.name: Tandoori Roti
steps: Reserve 30 g flour and 20 ml water. Knead remaining flour, salt, curd and remaining water for 6–8 minutes into a smooth, slightly firm dough.
Cover dough for 30 minutes. Preheat the oven to 250°C with a heavy oven-safe baking tray inside for at least 25 minutes.
Divide dough into eight balls. Roll with reserved flour to ovals about 4 mm thick; lightly brush one side with the reserved water.
Using oven gloves, place two or three rotis wet-side down on the hot tray. Bake 3–5 minutes until puffed and the underside is set.
Finish under the oven grill for 30–60 seconds if needed for brown blisters; watch continuously and keep the bread clear of the heating element.
Brush baked rotis with ghee. Tear one to check there is no gummy centre, and serve immediately; reheat the tray briefly between batches.
tips: Keep unused dough covered so the surface does not dry out.

recipe.notes: Home-oven adaptation of tandoori roti; eight rotis. A domestic oven gives browned blisters without a traditional tandoor.

recipe.name: Methi Paratha
steps: Pick fenugreek leaves from tough stems, wash well and dry thoroughly. Chop finely; reserve 30 g flour for rolling.
Mix remaining flour with leaves, salt, carom seeds, turmeric and chilli powder. Add curd, 10 g ghee and water gradually to make soft dough.
Rest covered for 20 minutes, then divide into eight balls. Roll one ball into a small disc and spread a thin film of ghee.
Fold the disc in half, grease lightly and fold again into a triangle. Roll gently with reserved flour to about 3 mm thick.
Heat a heavy tawa over medium-high heat. Cook a paratha for 60–90 seconds until bubbles appear, then turn and brush with a little ghee.
Turn again, grease the second side and press the edges. Cook 2–3 minutes more until browned on both sides with no damp dough at the edges.

recipe.name: Mooli Paratha
steps: Reserve 30 g flour for dusting. Knead the remaining flour with 4 g salt and the measured water into a soft dough; cover for 20 minutes.
Grate peeled radish, toss with remaining salt and stand for 10 minutes. Squeeze very firmly in a clean cloth; discard the extracted liquid.
Mix squeezed radish with finely chopped chilli and coriander, carom seeds and chilli powder. Stuff immediately, before the filling releases more moisture.
Divide dough and filling into eight equal portions. Roll each dough ball into a small disc, place filling centrally and pinch the edges closed.
Flatten seam-side down. Dust lightly with the reserved flour and roll gently to about 16 cm, keeping the filling evenly enclosed.
Heat a heavy tawa over medium-high heat. Cook a paratha for 60–90 seconds until bubbles appear, then turn and brush with a little ghee.
Turn again, grease the second side and press the edges. Cook 2–3 minutes more until browned on both sides with no damp dough at the edges.
tips: Keep unused dough covered so the surface does not dry out.
recipe.notes: Makes eight breads, two per serving. Serve freshly cooked with a curry or curd.

recipe.name: Amritsari Kulcha
steps: Reserve 100 ml water. Mix 300 g flour, curd, sugar, 4 g salt, baking powder, soda and 10 g ghee; knead with reserved water and rest covered 2 hours.
Boil potatoes in remaining water until knife-tender, about 25 minutes. Drain, peel, cool and mash; mix with finely chopped onion, chilli, coriander and remaining spices and salt.
Preheat an oven with a heavy oven-safe tray to 250°C for 25 minutes. Divide dough and cooled filling into eight portions.
Divide dough and filling into eight equal portions. Roll each dough ball into a small disc, place filling centrally and pinch the edges closed.
Dust with remaining flour and roll filled balls to 15 cm, about 5 mm thick. Press nigella seeds onto the tops.
Bake two at a time on the hot tray for 6–8 minutes until puffed and golden underneath. Grill tops briefly for brown spots, watching closely.
Brush with remaining ghee and serve hot. Check the edge of the first kulcha is cooked through, without a sticky flour layer around the filling.
tips: Keep unused dough covered so the surface does not dry out.
recipe.notes: Makes eight stuffed kulchas using a home oven. Onion and potato are traditional ingredients here; household choices determine suitability.

recipe.name: Malabar Parotta
steps: Mix flour, sugar and salt. Add water and 15 ml oil; knead vigorously for 10–12 minutes until very smooth and stretchy rather than sticky.
Coat dough with 5 ml oil and rest covered for 1 hour. Divide into eight balls, lightly oil and rest another 20 minutes.
Oil the worktop lightly. Stretch each ball into a very thin sheet using oiled hands; small tears are acceptable. Spread a little measured oil over it.
Pleat the sheet into a long ribbon, coil loosely and tuck the end underneath. Rest the coils covered for 15 minutes before gently flattening to 15 cm.
Cook on a medium-hot heavy tawa for about 2 minutes per side, using remaining oil sparingly. Flip repeatedly until layered edges are cooked and golden spots form.
Stack two or three hot parottas and press their edges inward with clean cloth-covered hands to separate the layers. Serve immediately while tender inside.
tips: Keep unused dough covered so the surface does not dry out.
recipe.notes: Makes eight layered parottas. This traditional-style version uses flour, water and oil without added dairy.

recipe.name: Kalakand
steps: Grease a small square tin with 3 g ghee. Crumble fresh paneer into fine, soft grains; do not knead it into a smooth paste.
Bring milk to a boil in a wide heavy pan. Reduce to medium-low and simmer 20–30 minutes, scraping the sides, until approximately half remains.
Add crumbled paneer and stir gently. Cook 10–15 minutes, frequently scraping the bottom, until the mixture is thick but still moist.
Add sugar and remaining ghee. Stir on low heat until released liquid evaporates and the mixture gathers together, leaving a thin moist trail on the pan.
Switch off and mix in cardamom. Spread into the greased tin about 2 cm thick, level lightly and press chopped pistachios onto the surface.
Cool for 30 minutes, then refrigerate for 2 hours until softly set. Cut into twelve pieces; the inside should remain moist and grainy, not rubbery.
tips: Use a heavy pan and scrape the base regularly to prevent scorching.
recipe.notes: Makes twelve small pieces, three per serving. Cool promptly, refrigerate in a covered container and use within 3 days.

recipe.name: Motichoor Ladoo
steps: Whisk gram flour with 230 ml water into a smooth, thin pouring batter. Rest 10 minutes; ready a fine-hole boondi ladle and a draining sieve.
Heat oil to 170°C in a deep pan. Hold the boondi ladle just above it and tap small ladlefuls of batter through, keeping hands clear.
Fry tiny pearls for 30–45 seconds, just until set without becoming crisp. Drain promptly and wipe the ladle clean between batches.
Boil sugar, saffron and remaining 100 ml water until a cooled drop draws one fine thread. Test only a cooled drop, never hot syrup, and turn off the heat at this stage.
Stir boondi into hot syrup with ghee, cardamom and melon seeds. Cover for 10 minutes so the pearls absorb syrup; stir once halfway through.
If pearls are too large, pulse the warm mixture very briefly, keeping visible grains. Let it cool until comfortable to handle, then press into twelve firm ladoos.
tips: A fine-hole ladle makes the characteristic tiny pearls; do not fry the boondi until crunchy.
recipe.passiveTime: 10 minutes batter resting and 10 minutes syrup absorption
recipe.notes: Makes twelve small ladoos. The oil quantity is a frying bath, not the amount eaten. Refrigerate cooled ladoos and use within 3 days.

recipe.name: Rava Ladoo
steps: Heat 15 g ghee in a heavy pan. Fry chopped cashews until pale golden, add raisins briefly until plump, and lift both onto a plate.
Add remaining ghee and semolina to the pan. Roast on low heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring continuously, until fragrant but still pale.
Add coconut and roast for 2 minutes more. Transfer to a broad bowl and cool until warm; very hot semolina will melt the sugar.
Mix in powdered sugar, cardamom and fried nuts and raisins. Rub gently between fingers to distribute the fat evenly without compacting the entire mixture.
Warm the measured milk and sprinkle it gradually over the mixture. Rest 5 minutes; a squeezed handful should hold together without dripping or feeling wet.
Divide into twelve portions and press firmly into balls while warm. Cool fully, then refrigerate because milk has been added; bring portions to room temperature before serving.
tips: Use a heavy pan and scrape the base regularly to prevent scorching.
recipe.notes: Makes twelve small pieces, three per serving. Cool promptly, refrigerate in a covered container and use within 3 days.

recipe.name: Doodh Peda
steps: Warm 30 ml milk and steep crushed saffron in it for 10 minutes. Grease a plate lightly using a little of the measured ghee.
Crumble the mawa finely into a heavy pan and mix with the remaining milk. Add sugar and the remaining ghee, then place over low heat and stir until evenly combined.
Stir continuously for 8–12 minutes, scraping the base and corners. Add saffron milk and cardamom once the mixture becomes a thick paste.
Continue cooking gently until the mixture pulls away as a soft mass. Cool a small dab on a plate: it should roll without sticking badly.
Transfer to the greased plate and cool until comfortably warm, about 15 minutes. Do not overcook to a dry crumble or the pedas will become hard.
Divide into twelve balls, flatten gently and press chopped pistachios into shallow central dents. Cool completely before refrigerating in a covered container.
tips: Use a heavy pan and scrape the base regularly to prevent scorching.
recipe.passiveTime: 10 minutes saffron soaking and 15 minutes cooling
recipe.notes: Makes twelve small saffron milk pedas using milk powder for a practical home method. Refrigerate and use within 3 days.

recipe.name: Soan Papdi
steps: Prepare a heatproof silicone mat, two sturdy spatulas and a small greased tin. Sift both flours; use 5 g ghee to grease the mat and tin.
Roast both flours in remaining ghee over low heat for 15–18 minutes until nutty and pale golden. Mix in cardamom and keep the flour paste warm.
Dissolve sugar in water, add lemon juice and boil without stirring to 140°C on a sugar thermometer. Do not test hot syrup with bare fingers.
Pour syrup carefully onto the mat. Using spatulas, fold edges inward as it cools, until the sugar is a pliable mass rather than flowing liquid.
When safe to handle with food-safe heat-resistant gloves, stretch and fold the sugar until opaque. Form a ring; never touch sugar that still burns through protection.
Coat the ring with warm roasted flour paste. Stretch wider, twist into a figure eight and fold together; repeat, coating strands with paste each time.
Continue until many fine strands separate and most paste is incorporated. Gather the strands into the tin without crushing them; scatter pistachios and press only lightly.
Score twelve pieces while just warm and cool fully for 1 hour before lifting. Store airtight in a cool, dry place; moisture makes the strands sticky.
tips: Keep the flour paste warm and work steadily; cold sugar snaps instead of forming fine fibres.
recipe.notes: Makes twelve small pieces. An advanced pulled-sugar recipe requiring a sugar thermometer, heatproof work surface and food-safe heat protection; texture depends on repeated pulling.

recipe.name: Milk Cake
steps: Grease a small deep metal tin with a little measured ghee. Mix lemon juice with the water. Use a wide heavy pan so milk can reduce without scorching.
Bring milk to a boil, then simmer for 35–45 minutes, stirring and scraping the base and sides, until roughly half remains. Keep returning the soft milk solids to the pan.
Add diluted lemon gradually while stirring until small grains form in the thick milk. Stop adding once grainy; do not separate it into dry curds and clear whey.
Add sugar and cook over low heat for 20–30 minutes, stirring constantly as it thickens. Add the remaining ghee gradually; the mixture should become beige, grainy and pull away from the pan.
Mix in cardamom and pack firmly into the greased tin; scatter chopped pistachio on top. Cover loosely and cool for 45 minutes, then refrigerate until firm for at least 2 hours.
Unmould with a thin knife and cut into small pieces. The texture should be moist and granular, with a deeper colour possible in the centre; keep leftovers refrigerated.
recipe.passiveTime: Cool for 45 minutes, then chill for at least 2 hours.
recipe.notes: Base recipe for 4 adults. Cooking times are estimates; follow the texture and doneness cues. Jain suitability follows your saved ingredient choices.

recipe.name: Gujiya
steps: Rub 30 g ghee into the flour until it resembles breadcrumbs and holds when squeezed. Add water gradually to form a firm dough; cover and rest for 25 minutes.
Crumble mawa and roast in the remaining ghee over low heat for 5–7 minutes until fragrant and slightly dry. Add coconut and chopped almonds for 1 minute, then cool completely.
Stir sugar, raisins and cardamom into the cool filling. Divide dough into 8 balls and roll each into a thin disc, keeping the unused dough covered to prevent drying.
Divide filling between discs, leaving a clean border. Moisten the rim lightly with water, fold into a half-moon and press and crimp firmly; trapped filling at the seam can make it open.
Heat frying oil to about 160°C in a deep pan no more than half full. Fry in batches for 12–15 minutes, turning gently, until evenly golden and the pastry feels crisp.
Drain on a rack and cool before serving; the filling stays very hot. Frying oil is a cooking medium, not an amount to consume. Refrigerate cooled leftovers because the filling contains dairy.

recipe.name: Modak
steps: Grate coconut and jaggery. Heat 5 g ghee, add both and cook over medium-low heat for 6–8 minutes until melted together and moist but not watery. Add cardamom and cool.
Boil the measured water with salt and 5 g ghee. Turn heat low, add rice flour all at once and stir firmly until no dry flour remains; cover off heat for 5 minutes.
When warm enough to handle, knead the dough until smooth, using damp hands. Divide into 8 balls and keep covered; if edges crack when pressed, knead in a few drops of warm water.
Use the remaining ghee on hands and steamer plate. Flatten each ball into a cup, add an equal share of filling, pleat the rim and bring the pleats together into a sealed pointed top.
Bring separate steamer water to a boil below the plate, without touching the modaks. Steam covered for 12–15 minutes until the shells look slightly glossy and feel set.
Rest off heat for 5 minutes before lifting with a damp spoon. Serve warm, taking care with the hot filling; refrigerate any cooled leftovers.

recipe.name: Coconut Barfi
steps: Grease a small shallow tray with a little measured ghee. Finely grate the white coconut flesh, avoiding large hard pieces, and chop the pistachio.
Put coconut and milk in a heavy pan and cook over medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring, until coconut softens and most loose milk has evaporated.
Add sugar and the remaining ghee. The mixture will loosen first; keep stirring for 12–18 minutes until it forms a cohesive mass that leaves the sides, without browning.
Stir in cardamom. Spread promptly in the greased tray, flatten with a greased spoon and press pistachio onto the surface. Score into small squares while still warm.
Cool for 30 minutes, then refrigerate for 1 hour to set before separating the pieces. Keep chilled in a covered container because fresh coconut and milk spoil quickly.

recipe.name: Balushahi
steps: Mix flour and baking soda, then rub in ghee until crumbly. Fold in curd and up to 40 ml of the measured water just until a rough dough forms; do not knead smooth.
Cover and rest for 25 minutes. Divide into 8 pieces, shape gently into thick rounds and make a shallow central dent; retain the fine surface cracks that create flaky layers.
Dissolve sugar in the remaining 120 ml water and bring to a simmer. Cook until a cooled drop feels sticky and forms a thin thread when stretched; stir in lemon juice and cardamom and keep warm.
Heat frying oil to 140–150°C in a deep pan no more than half full. Lower in a batch carefully and fry slowly for 20–25 minutes, turning occasionally, until puffed and evenly golden.
Drain on a rack and let stand for 5 minutes. Break one test piece to check the centre is cooked and layered, not a wet flour paste; continue frying if necessary.
Dip the warm pieces in warm syrup for 2 minutes on each side. Lift onto a rack and cool until the glaze sets; the listed frying oil is a cooking medium, not a serving quantity.
